A content delivery network is a system of computers spread across many cities that store copies of websites and videos so people can load them faster. Normally, every request travels back to one main computer, called the origin server, where the website's files originally live. If that computer is far away, pages load slowly. To fix this, copies of the content get placed on servers closer to visitors, called edge locations, since they sit near the "edge" of the network, close to homes and offices rather than in one distant data center. When a request arrives, the nearby edge location checks whether it already has a saved copy; finding one is called a cache hit, and it means the answer can be delivered instantly without contacting the origin server at all. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood bakeries that all sell bread baked at one central factory: instead of everyone driving across town to the factory, each bakery keeps fresh loaves on hand, so most customers get served immediately from the nearest shop. Only when a bakery runs out does it need to call the factory for more, which takes extra time. This is why streaming, shopping, and news sites feel fast regardless of where people are located: most requests get answered nearby, and only occasional ones travel all the way back to the source.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer storing the real website files | Everything ultimately comes from here |
| Edge location | A nearby server holding copies of the content | Shortens the distance data must travel |
| Cache hit | A successful request answered from a stored copy | Delivers instant results without extra travel |
| Cache miss | A request that isn't found nearby and must reach origin | Explains occasional slower loads |
